lines.watchItem: Advanced-packaging allocation is again described as the binding limit on AI system availability, with lead times of roughly 52 to 78 weeks against capacity of about 105,000 to 130,000 wafers per month by the fourth quarter of 2026. The exposure is that packaged output, not wafer output, sets how much accelerator revenue the chain can realize.

Advanced-packaging capacity is pre-booked at more than 85 percent for 2026 and 2027, with one customer at roughly 60 percent of 2026 capacity and the top three customers above 85 percent of total capacity. That concentration means a single buyer trimming orders leaves slots that are hard to refill.

Leading-node loading is still running ahead of build-out: August 2026 revenue rose 53.3 percent year over year, the company says it cannot meet current demand while building about 20 plants at once, and its own quarterly tool demand has climbed to roughly 1.9 times the level projected in December 2025. Construction labour and equipment delivery are the named pacing items to watch.

Memory now caps how much of the accelerator ramp converts into shipments: the leading vendor guided fiscal 2028 growth to about 70 percent against customer forecasts implying roughly 140 percent, citing memory, while supplier stockpiles have fallen below ten days. Wafer and packaging plans booked against the unconstrained demand figure carry the risk of sitting idle behind the memory limit.

The leading-node customer base is broadening from merchant accelerator vendors toward custom parts, with custom chip growth projected at 44.6 percent versus 16.1 percent for merchant GPUs and 27.8 percent of the server market in 2026, Microsoft negotiating capacity for upward of 300,000 Maia 300 chips, and OpenAI's first inference chip built on a 3nm process. The mix shift changes which customers hold the wafers rather than the total pulled.

Margin along the chain is moving toward the memory makers: the leading accelerator vendor's gross margin steps down from 75 percent toward a stated 71 to 72 percent floor on memory costs and it is raising AI server prices by more than 15 percent, while TSMC reported a 67.7 percent gross margin with 2026 revenue growth guided above 40 percent. Watch whether buyers keep absorbing component pass-through or start capping it.

A second packaging route is forming around Intel's bridge technology, with reported yield above 90 percent at roughly half the cost of CoWoS, a Google order for more than 3 million units for 2028 delivery, and Intel at about 13.7 percent of 2.5D capacity against TSMC near 70 percent. The route is described as a better fit for custom chips than for high-bandwidth accelerators, so the near-term exposure sits in custom-silicon packaging share.

Policy is tying capacity location to market access: planned Arizona investment now totals $265 billion, while Washington is preparing semiconductor tariffs extending to finished servers with duty-free allowances sized to each company's US fabrication investment, and no rate or start date has been set. The open question is how the allowance formula treats investment already committed.
